Sri Lankan Unrest Disrupts Trade and Daily Life as Crisis Deepens

COLOMBO, June 25 — Widespread political unrest across Sri Lanka has brought much of the island nation’s economic activity to a near standstill, with street protests, transport disruptions, and a growing sense of uncertainty as talks between rival political factions stalled on Tuesday.

The crisis, which began over the weekend after weeks of mounting tension between government forces and opposition groups, has seen sporadic clashes in Colombo and other major cities. Demonstrators demanding new elections and government accountability have blocked key highways and the entry to Colombo’s main commercial port, causing significant delays to shipments and disrupting supply chains.

The Sri Lankan Chamber of Commerce reported that shipments at the Port of Colombo, a vital transshipment hub for South Asia, have dropped by 60% since Saturday. “Exporters and importers are facing severe delays, and perishable goods are at risk,” said Chamber President Dinesh Aluthgama in a statement. “If this continues, there will be long-term damage to Sri Lanka’s reputation as a reliable trading partner.”

Banks and ATMs in several urban centers remained closed on Tuesday, and transport unions said bus and train services had been cut by half due to fuel shortages and safety concerns for drivers. “Our members are unwilling to risk their lives while streets are blocked by protesters and police,” said Sarath Kumara, spokesperson for the United Transport Workers’ Association.

The unrest has also triggered panic buying of essentials, with residents reporting hours-long lines outside grocery stores and pharmacies. “We haven’t seen shelves this empty since the economic crisis two years ago,” said Anjali Perera, a resident of Galle. “People are worried the situation will get worse before it gets better.”

The Central Bank of Sri Lanka warned on Tuesday that prolonged instability could further weaken the rupee and worsen inflation, which stood at 8.5% in May. “Business confidence is already fragile, and these events could have lasting effects,” said independent economist Ruwan Gunatillake.

President Mahinda Weerasinghe called for calm but has so far failed to reach an agreement with opposition leaders on a path forward. The United Nations urged all sides to respect human rights and begin urgent dialogue.

As the crisis enters its fourth day, analysts warn that unless a political resolution is found, Sri Lanka’s economic recovery from the pandemic and last year’s financial turmoil could face a severe setback.
